specStatements.text: Momentum is defined by the equation:
momentum, p, in kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s
In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.
This is called conservation of momentum.
Students should be able to use the concept of momentum as a model to:
• describe and explain examples of momentum in a n event, such as a collision
• (physics only) complete calculations involving an event, such as the collision of two objects.
When a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, a change in momentum occurs.
The equations F = m × a and a = (v - u)/(t)
combine to give the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)
where m ∆ v = change in momentum
ie force equals the rate of change of momentum.

Students should be able to explain safety features such as: air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned surfaces for playgrounds with reference to the concept of rate of change of momentum.
Students should be able to apply equations relating force, mass, velocity and acceleration to explain how the changes involved are inter-related.

scopeNotes.statement: • (physics only) complete calculations involving an event, such as the collision of two objects.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification restricts the calculation of an event to the separate GCSE Physics course; students taking GCSE Combined Science are required only to describe and explain examples of momentum in an event. Every calculation item here (q12, q14, q15, q16) is therefore flagged in this note as physics-only material, and none of it is treated as a prerequisite for the qualitative statements in 4.5.7.2. The qualitative work — describing what happens to momentum in a collision, and explaining it — is carried by items that need no arithmetic at all (c11, m07, m10, q10, q11, q13), so a combined science student can meet the whole of their requirement without touching the calculation items. The calculations themselves stay inside the specification's own example: an event such as the collision of two objects, in one dimension, in a closed system. No two-dimensional momentum, no vector diagrams, and no algebraic treatment of a general collision are introduced.

The whole of section 4.5.7 is Higher Tier only, so every concept, misconception and question in this material is tagged tier 'higher' and none of it is presented as Foundation content. Nothing here is required of a Foundation student, and no item assumes a Foundation student has met momentum. The material also stays inside the Higher Tier boundary in the other direction: the term 'impulse' is never used, because the specification does not name it; kinetic energy is not used to classify collisions as elastic or inelastic, because the specification does not ask for that distinction; and momentum is treated only along a single line, with one direction taken as positive, which is all the specification's own example of a collision of two objects requires.

concepts.definition: A property of a moving object. The specification defines momentum by an equation: momentum is the object's mass multiplied by its velocity. Because velocity appears in the definition, an object has momentum only while it is moving — a stationary object has zero momentum however large its mass is.

The word equation that defines momentum. In the AQA list of equations this is one that students are required to recall, so it must be learned rather than looked up. Both quantities on the right must be in SI units before it is used: mass in kilograms and velocity in metres per second.

The symbol form of the momentum equation: p is momentum, m is mass and v is velocity. It rearranges to m = p / v and to v = p / m, so any one of the three quantities can be found when the other two are known.

Momentum, p, in kilograms metre per second, kg m/s. The unit follows directly from the equation: kilograms (mass) multiplied by metres per second (velocity). It is not the newton, which is the unit of force, and not the joule, which is the unit of energy.

Mass, m, in kilograms, kg. A mass given in grams must be converted to kilograms before p = m v is used — divide by 1000. A value in newtons is a weight, not a mass, and cannot be substituted into the equation.
Velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s. Velocity is the speed of the object in a given direction, so the number substituted into p = m v carries a direction with it.

Because momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, and velocity has a direction, momentum has a direction too. For objects moving along one line, choose one direction as positive; anything moving the other way then has a negative velocity and so a negative momentum. Two objects of equal mass moving towards each other at the same speed have momenta that cancel to zero.

A system that nothing enters and nothing leaves, and on which no external force acts. Conservation of momentum is stated by the specification for a closed system, so the two colliding trolleys, or the two skaters, must be considered together and treated as free from outside forces such as a push from a hand.

The momenta of all the objects in the system added together, with direction taken into account. An object moving in the negative direction contributes a negative amount, so the total can be smaller than either individual momentum, and can be zero.

In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event. This is called conservation of momentum. It is what makes an unknown velocity after a collision findable: total momentum after must equal the total worked out before.

concepts.term: Momentum as a model for an event
concepts.definition: An event is anything that changes how the objects in a system are moving — most often a collision. Momentum is used as a model for such an event: individual objects gain or lose momentum, but the total for the closed system does not change, so any momentum one object loses has been transferred to the other.

concepts.term: Collision in which the objects join
concepts.definition: When two objects collide and move off together, they afterwards have one combined mass and one shared velocity. Total momentum before is worked out from the separate objects; total momentum after is the combined mass multiplied by that shared velocity, and the two totals are equal.

If two objects are stationary and then push each other apart, the total momentum before the event is zero, so the total afterwards must also be zero. The two objects therefore move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size — which means the lighter object moves off with the greater speed.

When a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, a change in momentum occurs. The change is written m ∆v, where ∆v is the change in velocity — the final velocity minus the initial velocity — not the final velocity itself. A car of mass 1200 kg slowing from 20 m/s to rest has a change in momentum of 1200 × 20 = 24 000 kg m/s.

Force equals the change in momentum divided by the time taken for that change. Force, F, in newtons, N; m ∆v is the change in momentum in kg m/s; ∆t is the time in seconds, s. This equation is provided on the AQA Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled, but it does have to be selected and used correctly.

concepts.term: Force as the rate of change of momentum
concepts.definition: 'Rate of change of momentum' means the change in momentum divided by the time taken, not the total momentum divided by the time. Force equals that rate: for one fixed change in momentum, the longer the change takes, the smaller the force.

concepts.term: Combining F = m × a with a = (v − u)/t
concepts.definition: Substituting the acceleration equation into the force equation gives F = m(v − u)/t. Since (v − u) is the change in velocity, ∆v, and t is the time for that change, ∆t, this is F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). The momentum equation is not a new law — it is Newton's Second Law written in terms of momentum.

concepts.term: Increasing the time of a collision
concepts.definition: In a crash or a landing, the change in momentum is fixed by how fast the person was going and by their mass — it cannot be reduced by the safety feature. What the safety feature changes is ∆t. Increasing the time taken for the momentum to fall to zero reduces m ∆v ÷ ∆t, and so reduces the force on the person.

Air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned surfaces for playgrounds all work the same way: they deform, stretch or squash, so the person is brought to rest over a longer time. The rate of change of momentum is smaller, so the force on the person is smaller.

Force, mass, velocity and acceleration are linked through F = m a, a = (v − u)/t and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). Holding the change in momentum fixed and making the time five times longer makes the force five times smaller; holding the time fixed and doubling the change in velocity doubles the force. Explaining a safety feature means saying which quantity is held fixed and which one has been changed.

misconceptions.question: A bullet travels much faster than a lorry. Does the bullet have the greater momentum?
misconceptions.correct: No. Momentum is mass × velocity, and the lorry's enormous mass more than makes up for its low speed.
misconceptions.misconception: Whichever object is moving faster must have the more momentum — momentum is basically about speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language 'momentum' is used to mean something like unstoppable speed, and the examples students meet first (a fast ball, a speeding car) vary the speed while leaving the mass unmentioned.
misconceptions.correction: Always calculate. Multiply mass by velocity for each object and compare the two numbers; a large mass at a small velocity often wins.

misconceptions.question: A 8000 kg lorry crawls at 2 m/s while a 1000 kg car does 20 m/s. Which has the greater momentum?
misconceptions.correct: The car: 1000 × 20 = 20 000 kg m/s, compared with 8000 × 2 = 16 000 kg m/s for the lorry.
misconceptions.misconception: The heavier object always has the greater momentum, because momentum is about how massive something is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass is the first quantity in the equation and the most vivid feature of a lorry, so students compare the masses and stop there instead of completing the multiplication.
misconceptions.correction: Neither quantity decides on its own. Work out mass × velocity for both objects before making any comparison.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of momentum?
misconceptions.correct: Kilograms metre per second, kg m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is measured in newtons, because it is to do with the force something hits you with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Momentum is introduced alongside force, and the everyday sense of momentum is 'how hard something hits'. The newton is the unit students associate with impact.
misconceptions.correction: Build the unit from the equation: kilograms multiplied by metres per second gives kg m/s. Newtons belong to force, which is the rate of change of momentum, not momentum itself.

misconceptions.question: A 60 kg sprinter runs at 8 m/s. Is the momentum 240 kg m/s?
misconceptions.correct: No. Momentum is 60 × 8 = 480 kg m/s. There is no factor of one half in p = m v.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is worked out like kinetic energy — you halve it, or you square the velocity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Kinetic energy, ½ m v², is met earlier in the same topic and also contains mass and velocity, so the two equations blur together and the ½ or the squaring migrates across.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two apart: kinetic energy is ½ m v² in joules; momentum is m v in kg m/s. Momentum has no ½ and the velocity is not squared.

misconceptions.question: A parked 12 000 kg lorry — how much momentum does it have?
misconceptions.correct: None. Its velocity is zero, so p = 12 000 × 0 = 0 kg m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: Something that heavy must have a lot of momentum sitting in it, ready to be released.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Momentum is talked about as if it were a possession, like mass, rather than something that depends on motion. A parked lorry still feels 'powerful'.
misconceptions.correction: Momentum depends on velocity as well as mass. Zero velocity gives zero momentum, no matter how large the mass.

misconceptions.question: A 0.5 kg ball moving right at 4 m/s meets a 0.3 kg ball moving left at 2 m/s. What is the total momentum?
misconceptions.correct: Taking right as positive: 2.0 + (−0.6) = 1.4 kg m/s to the right.
misconceptions.misconception: You add the two momenta together, so the total is 2.6 kg m/s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Total' is read as 'add everything up'. Direction has been carried through velocity all year, but with a new quantity students revert to treating the numbers as plain sizes.
misconceptions.correction: Momentum has direction because velocity does. Choose one direction as positive, make the opposite one negative, and then add.

misconceptions.question: Two trolleys collide, join together and move off slowly. Has momentum been lost?
misconceptions.correct: No. The combined trolley has a larger mass, so the same total momentum is carried at a smaller velocity.
misconceptions.misconception: They are moving much more slowly afterwards, so some of the momentum has been used up or destroyed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge momentum by how fast things are moving and see the drop in speed as a drop in momentum. Energy really is dissipated in such a collision, which reinforces the idea that something has been lost.
misconceptions.correction: Check with numbers. Mass before is 2 kg at 3 m/s, giving 6 kg m/s; mass afterwards is 3 kg at 2 m/s, also 6 kg m/s. The total is unchanged in a closed system.

misconceptions.question: A rolling ball slows to a stop against a rough carpet. Is momentum conserved?
misconceptions.correct: Not for the ball alone. Friction from the carpet is an external force, so the ball on its own is not a closed system.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is always conserved, in every situation, whatever else is going on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is remembered as a slogan — 'momentum is conserved' — with the opening words 'in a closed system' dropped as scene-setting rather than a condition.
misconceptions.correction: Quote the statement in full: in a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event. If an external force acts, the condition is not met.

misconceptions.question: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they join. What velocity do you divide the momentum by?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the 6 kg m/s by the combined mass of 3 kg, giving 2 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: You divide by 2 kg, because that is the trolley that was moving and so the one that has the momentum.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The stationary trolley contributed nothing before the collision, so students carry on ignoring it afterwards, even though it is now part of the moving object.
misconceptions.correction: After the objects join there is one object. Its mass is the sum of the two masses, and that is what the total momentum is divided by.

misconceptions.question: Two skaters of different mass push apart from rest. Do they move off at the same speed?
misconceptions.correct: No. Their momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the lighter skater moves off faster.
misconceptions.misconception: They pushed each other equally hard, so they must both end up going at the same speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The forces on the two skaters really are equal in size, and students slide from equal forces to equal speeds without going through mass.
misconceptions.correction: Equal and opposite momenta, not equal speeds. Set 60 × 1.5 equal to 45 × v and solve: v = 2 m/s, faster than the heavier skater.

misconceptions.question: A car of mass 1200 kg stops from 20 m/s in 0.10 s. Is the force 24 000 N?
misconceptions.correct: No. 24 000 kg m/s is the change in momentum; the force is 24 000 ÷ 0.10 = 240 000 N.
misconceptions.misconception: Force is the change in momentum — you work out m ∆v and that is the answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Force equals the rate of change of momentum' is compressed in memory to 'force equals change of momentum', and m ∆v is the part of the equation that gets calculated first.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). The division by time is what turns a change in momentum into a force, and it is what makes the units newtons rather than kg m/s.

misconceptions.question: What does 'rate of change of momentum' mean?
misconceptions.correct: The change in momentum divided by the time taken for that change.
misconceptions.misconception: It means the momentum the object has, divided by the time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Rate of' is correctly read as 'divided by time', but 'change of' is skipped, so the total momentum is used where the change should be.
misconceptions.correction: Two steps every time: first find the change in momentum, m ∆v, then divide by ∆t. For an object slowing from 20 m/s to 15 m/s, ∆v is 5 m/s, not 15 m/s.

misconceptions.question: In F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what is ∆v for a car slowing from 20 m/s to 12 m/s?
misconceptions.correct: ∆v is the change in velocity, 20 − 12 = 8 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: ∆v is the velocity the car ends up with, so it is 12 m/s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The delta symbol is new and easily read as decoration on the letter v rather than as an instruction to subtract. Many earlier equations do use the final velocity directly.
misconceptions.correction: ∆ always means 'change in'. Write down the initial and final velocities and subtract before substituting anything.

misconceptions.question: Does an air bag reduce the driver's change in momentum in a crash?
misconceptions.correct: No. The driver still goes from full speed to rest, so m ∆v is the same. The air bag increases ∆t.
misconceptions.misconception: The air bag makes the change in momentum smaller, and that is why the force is smaller.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the safety feature makes the crash gentler and attach that to the only quantity in the equation they can name, without noticing that the driver's speed before the crash and their speed afterwards are both fixed.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what the driver's velocity is before and after: unchanged by the bag. Only the time is changed, and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) then gives a smaller force.

misconceptions.question: Does a crash mat work by stopping the gymnast more quickly?
misconceptions.correct: No — the opposite. The mat squashes, so the gymnast takes longer to stop and the force on them is smaller.
misconceptions.misconception: Safety features bring you to a stop faster, and stopping fast is what keeps you safe.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Safety is associated with braking quickly from road-safety teaching about stopping distances, so 'stops you quickly' sounds like a virtue in any context.
misconceptions.correction: Stopping quickly means a large rate of change of momentum, which means a large force. Every one of the safety features named works by stretching the stopping time out.

misconceptions.question: Does a cycle helmet absorb the force of an impact?
misconceptions.correct: The helmet's foam crushes, so the head is brought to rest over a longer time and the force on the head is reduced.
misconceptions.misconception: The helmet soaks up the force and holds it, so less of it reaches you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Force is imagined as a substance that flows and can be stored, like water in a sponge. The word 'absorb' is used loosely in adverts and in everyday talk about padding.
misconceptions.correction: Force is an interaction, not a substance, and cannot be stored. Explain in terms of time: the crushing foam extends ∆t, so F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) is smaller.

misconceptions.question: A car doubles its velocity. What happens to its momentum?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles. Momentum is proportional to velocity, since p = m v.
misconceptions.misconception: It becomes four times as big, because doubling the velocity has a squared effect.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Kinetic energy really does quadruple when velocity doubles, and that striking fact is taught in the same unit. Students carry the squared relationship over to momentum.
misconceptions.correction: Look at the equation. Velocity appears to the power one in p = m v, so momentum simply doubles; it is ½ m v² that quadruples.

misconceptions.question: A ball weighs 5 N and moves at 4 m/s. Is its momentum 20 kg m/s?
misconceptions.correct: No. 5 N is a weight, not a mass. The mass must be found first, and it is the mass that goes into p = m v.
misconceptions.misconception: The number in newtons tells you how heavy the object is, so it can go straight into the momentum equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Weight' and 'mass' are interchangeable in everyday speech, and both are stated as single numbers describing how heavy something is.
misconceptions.correction: Check the unit before substituting. Mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; a value in newtons is a force and must be converted using weight = mass × gravitational field strength.

misconceptions.question: Is momentum equal to mass × acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: No. Momentum is mass × velocity. Mass × acceleration gives the resultant force.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is mass × acceleration, because momentum is about something speeding up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: F = m a and p = m v are met close together, both begin with mass, and 'momentum' sounds like the everyday idea of building up speed — which is acceleration.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two: mass × velocity is momentum, in kg m/s; mass × acceleration is resultant force, in newtons. An object at constant velocity has momentum but no acceleration.

misconceptions.question: A 250 g ball travels at 6 m/s. Is its momentum 1500 kg m/s?
misconceptions.correct: No. 250 g is 0.25 kg, so the momentum is 0.25 × 6 = 1.5 kg m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: You can put the mass into p = m v in whatever unit it is given in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as an arithmetic instruction, and the numbers given in a question feel authorised for use. Nothing in the calculation itself fails to warn the student.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states mass, m, in kilograms, kg. Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000 before substituting anything.

misconceptions.question: In p = m v, what does p stand for?
misconceptions.correct: Momentum. The specification gives momentum the symbol p.
misconceptions.misconception: p stands for power, or for pressure — those are what p means in physics.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The letter p is genuinely used for both power and pressure elsewhere in the course, and momentum has no obvious link to the letter p, so the older meanings win.
misconceptions.correction: Learn this symbol list as a set: momentum, p, in kg m/s; mass, m, in kg; velocity, v, in m/s. The unit is the giveaway — kg m/s can only be momentum.

misconceptions.question: In p = m v, is v the volume of the object?
misconceptions.correct: No, v is velocity, in metres per second.
misconceptions.misconception: v means volume, so momentum is worked out from mass and volume, like density.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Density, ρ = m/V, is met in the same course and uses m and V together, so a formula containing m and v looks like a version of it.
misconceptions.correction: Check the units the specification gives: velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s. Volume would give a unit of kg m³, which is not the unit of momentum.

misconceptions.question: A 900 kg van has 3600 kg m/s of momentum. Is its velocity 900 ÷ 3600?
misconceptions.correct: No. Rearranging p = m v gives v = p / m, so the velocity is 3600 ÷ 900 = 4 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: When you rearrange, you divide the smaller number into the bigger one, or divide mass by momentum.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearrangement is done by pattern-matching rather than algebra, and dividing whichever way produces a tidy number feels like a check that it was done correctly.
misconceptions.correction: Rearrange the symbols first, then substitute: v = p / m. Then test the units — kg m/s divided by kg leaves m/s, which is a velocity.

misconceptions.question: A braking force acts on a moving van. Is its momentum changing?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A change in momentum occurs whenever a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move — here the momentum is decreasing.
misconceptions.misconception: A force can only give an object more momentum; slowing down is momentum being lost rather than changed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Forces are introduced as things that get objects going, and 'change' is heard as 'increase'. A decrease looks like the absence of a change rather than a change with the opposite sign.
misconceptions.correction: A change in momentum can be an increase or a decrease. The direction of the force decides which: a force opposing the motion reduces the momentum.

mcqs.stem: The specification defines momentum by an equation. Which word equation is that definition?

options.text: momentum = mass × velocity
options.rationale: This is the defining equation given in 4.5.7.1, and it is one of the equations students are required to recall.

options.text: momentum = mass × acceleration
options.rationale: Chosen by students who blend p = m v with F = m a; both start with mass and are taught days apart.

options.text: momentum = weight × velocity
options.rationale: Picked by students who treat weight and mass as the same 'how heavy' quantity.

options.text: momentum = force × velocity
options.rationale: Selected by students who associate momentum with the force of an impact rather than with mass.

mcqs.stem: The momentum equation is written in symbols as p = m v. What do p, m and v stand for?

options.text: power, mass and velocity
options.rationale: p is used for power elsewhere in the course, so the familiar meaning is carried over to a new equation.

options.text: momentum, mass and velocity
options.rationale: The specification states momentum, p; mass, m; velocity, v, and these are the only meanings that give the unit kg m/s.

options.text: pressure, mass and velocity
options.rationale: The other established meaning of p in physics; students who cannot place the symbol pick whichever they met most recently.

options.text: momentum, mass and volume
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read m and v as the pair from the density equation.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the unit of momentum given in the specification?

options.text: the newton, N, the same unit as force
options.rationale: Momentum is thought of as the force of an impact, so the unit of force is taken as its unit.

options.text: the joule, J, the same unit as energy
options.rationale: Selected by students who cannot separate momentum from kinetic energy, which does have joules.

options.text: the kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
options.rationale: The unit follows from the equation: kilograms multiplied by metres per second gives kg m/s, exactly as the specification states.

options.text: the metre per second, m/s, as for speed
options.rationale: Picked by students who think of momentum as essentially a measure of how fast something is going.

mcqs.stem: A ball of mass 250 g is travelling at 6 m/s. What is its momentum?

options.text: 1500 kg m/s
options.rationale: The mass is used in grams without converting: 250 × 6.

options.text: 0.75 kg m/s
options.rationale: The mass is converted correctly but a factor of one half is imported from the kinetic energy equation.

options.text: 0.042 kg m/s
options.rationale: The mass is divided by the velocity instead of multiplied, an error made when 0.25 and 6 seem the wrong way round.

options.text: 1.5 kg m/s
options.rationale: 250 g is 0.25 kg, and 0.25 × 6 = 1.5 kg m/s, with the mass in kilograms as the specification requires.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the units used in p = m v is correct?

options.text: The velocity must be in m/s and the mass in kg.
options.rationale: The specification gives mass, m, in kilograms, kg and velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s, which together give momentum in kg m/s.

options.text: The velocity must be in km/h and the mass in kg.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who take the units used on the road as the standard ones for vehicle problems.

options.text: The velocity must be in m/s and the mass in g.
options.rationale: Grams are the unit masses are usually quoted in at school, so they are assumed to be acceptable here.

options.text: The velocity must be in m/s and the mass in N.
options.rationale: Picked by students who treat a weight in newtons as the object's mass.

mcqs.stem: A sprinter of mass 60 kg is running at 8 m/s. What is the sprinter's momentum?

options.text: 240 kg m/s
options.rationale: A factor of one half has been carried across from ½ m v².

options.text: 480 kg m/s
options.rationale: p = m v = 60 × 8 = 480 kg m/s, with both quantities already in SI units.

options.text: 3840 kg m/s
options.rationale: The velocity has been squared, as it is in the kinetic energy equation: 60 × 8².

options.text: 7.5 kg m/s
options.rationale: The mass has been divided by the velocity rather than multiplied by it.

mcqs.stem: A lorry of mass 8000 kg is moving at 2 m/s. A car of mass 1000 kg is moving at 20 m/s. Which has the greater momentum?

options.text: The lorry, because its mass is eight times larger.
options.rationale: The masses are compared and the multiplication is never completed; mass is the more vivid quantity.

options.text: They are equal, as the mass and speed compensate.
options.rationale: Assumes the larger mass and the larger velocity must cancel exactly, without checking that 8 and 10 are different factors.

options.text: The car, because 1000 × 20 gives 20 000 kg m/s.
options.rationale: The car's 20 000 kg m/s beats the lorry's 8000 × 2 = 16 000 kg m/s: both quantities have to be multiplied.

options.text: The car, because it is travelling ten times faster.
options.rationale: Reaches the right object by the wrong route — speed alone is treated as deciding momentum.

mcqs.stem: A van of mass 900 kg has a momentum of 3600 kg m/s. What is its velocity?

options.rationale: The rearrangement is inverted: mass divided by momentum instead of momentum divided by mass.

options.text: 8 m/s
options.rationale: Comes from treating momentum as ½ m v and so doubling the correct answer.
The momentum value is copied out as though it were the velocity, with no division carried out.

options.text: 4 m/s
options.rationale: Rearranging p = m v gives v = p / m = 3600 ÷ 900 = 4 m/s, and kg m/s ÷ kg leaves m/s.

mcqs.stem: A student works out the momentum of a trolley and writes the answer as '12 N'. What is wrong with this?

options.text: The unit should be kg m/s, since momentum is mass × velocity.
options.rationale: Multiplying kilograms by metres per second gives kilograms metre per second, the unit the specification states for momentum.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; momentum is a force, so newtons are right.
options.rationale: Momentum is being treated as the force with which something hits, so its unit is taken to be the newton.

options.text: The unit should be joules, since momentum is a form of energy.
options.rationale: Selected by students who have merged momentum with kinetic energy.

options.text: The unit should be m/s, because momentum measures how fast it goes.
options.rationale: Chosen by students for whom momentum is essentially speed, so the mass drops out of the unit.

mcqs.stem: Which of these completes the specification's statement of conservation of momentum correctly?

options.text: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is greater than the total after it.
options.rationale: Fits the everyday impression that collisions use momentum up, especially when the objects end up moving slowly.

options.text: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total after it.
options.rationale: This is the statement given in 4.5.7.2, with both the closed-system condition and the equality intact.

options.text: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is shared equally after it.
options.rationale: Picked by students who think a collision must divide the motion evenly between the objects.

options.text: In any system at all, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total after it.
options.rationale: Remembers the equality but drops the closed-system condition, which is where friction and other external forces are excluded.

mcqs.stem: What name does the specification give to the rule that the total momentum of a closed system is the same before and after an event?

options.text: Newton's Second Law of motion
options.rationale: Students who confuse p = m v with F = m a attach the collision rule to the law that equation belongs to.

options.text: the principle of moments
options.rationale: 'Momentum' and 'moments' look and sound alike, and both are rules about a quantity staying balanced.

options.text: the conservation of momentum
options.rationale: The specification states directly: this is called conservation of momentum.

options.text: the conservation of energy
options.rationale: Chosen by students who do not distinguish momentum from energy; conservation of energy is the better-known rule.

mcqs.stem: Trolley A has a mass of 2 kg and moves at 3 m/s towards a stationary 1 kg trolley B. The two trolleys form a closed system. What is their total momentum immediately after the collision?

options.text: 9 kg m/s
options.rationale: The combined mass of 3 kg is multiplied by the original 3 m/s, as though the speed were unaffected.

options.text: 3 kg m/s
options.rationale: The total is halved on the assumption that a collision shares the motion out between the two trolleys.

options.text: 0 kg m/s
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe a collision uses momentum up, particularly when things end up moving slowly.

options.text: 6 kg m/s
options.rationale: Before the event the total is 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s, and in a closed system the total afterwards is equal to it.

mcqs.stem: A moving snooker ball strikes a stationary ball of equal mass head-on and stops dead. Which description of this event is correct?

options.text: All the momentum has been transferred to the second ball.
options.rationale: The total must be unchanged, so the momentum the first ball lost is now carried by the second, which has the same mass and so the same speed.

options.text: The momentum of the first ball has simply disappeared.
options.rationale: The ball that was being watched has stopped, so its momentum is treated as gone rather than passed on.

options.text: Both balls now share the momentum equally between them.
options.rationale: Sharing feels like the fair outcome of a collision, and it contradicts the stated fact that the first ball stops.

options.text: The second ball gains twice the momentum the first had.
options.rationale: Comes from adding a supposed 'push back' to the transfer, which would make the total after the event larger than before.

mcqs.stem: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley, and the two move off joined together. What is their velocity after the collision?

options.text: 3 m/s
options.rationale: The total momentum of 6 kg m/s is divided by 2 kg — the mass of the trolley that was moving — instead of by the combined 3 kg.

options.text: 2 m/s
options.rationale: Momentum before is 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s; after the collision the moving mass is 3 kg, so 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s.

options.text: 6 m/s
options.rationale: The total momentum in kg m/s is written down as if it were the velocity, with no division at all.
The original speed is halved on the idea that the two trolleys share the motion equally.

mcqs.stem: A 0.5 kg ball moving to the right at 4 m/s meets a 0.3 kg ball moving to the left at 2 m/s. Taking right as the positive direction, what is the total momentum of the two balls before they collide?

options.text: 2.6 kg m/s to the right
options.rationale: The two momenta are added as plain sizes: 2.0 + 0.6, with the leftward direction ignored.

options.text: 0.8 kg m/s to the right
options.rationale: The masses are subtracted first and the difference multiplied by 4 m/s, treating mass as the quantity that decides everything.

options.text: 1.4 kg m/s to the right
options.rationale: The momenta are +2.0 kg m/s and −0.6 kg m/s, and 2.0 − 0.6 = 1.4 kg m/s in the positive, rightward direction.

options.text: 1.4 kg m/s to the left
options.rationale: The right size, but the sign convention has been applied the wrong way round when stating the direction.

mcqs.stem: Two skaters stand at rest on ice and push each other apart. One has a mass of 60 kg and moves off at 1.5 m/s. The other has a mass of 45 kg. What is her velocity?

options.rationale: Equal pushes are taken to mean equal speeds, so the first skater's velocity is copied across.
The mass ratio is inverted: 45/60 × 1.5 instead of 60/45 × 1.5.

options.text: 90 m/s
options.rationale: Her momentum, 90 kg m/s, is found correctly but then reported as a velocity, with no division by 45 kg.

options.text: 2 m/s
options.rationale: Total momentum before is zero, so 60 × 1.5 = 45 × v, giving v = 2 m/s in the opposite direction.

mcqs.stem: The specification states what happens when a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move. What occurs?

options.text: a change in the momentum of the object
options.rationale: This is the statement in 4.5.7.3, and it holds whether the momentum increases or decreases.

options.text: a change in the weight of the object
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read any statement about a force as a statement about weight.

options.text: an increase in momentum, never a decrease
options.rationale: Forces are learned as things that get objects going, so 'change' is heard as 'increase'.

options.text: no change of momentum until it stops
options.rationale: Treats momentum as changing only at the end of the motion rather than throughout the time the force acts.

mcqs.stem: Which two equations does the specification combine to give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)?

options.text: E = ½ m v² and a = (v − u)/t
options.rationale: Picked by students who reach for the kinetic energy equation whenever mass and velocity appear together.

options.text: F = m × a and a = (v − u)/t
options.rationale: Substituting a = (v − u)/t into F = m × a gives F = m(v − u)/t, which is F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

options.text: W = F s and a = (v − u)/t
options.rationale: The work equation also contains F, so it looks like a plausible source of the F in the result.

options.text: p = m v and a = (v − u)/t
options.rationale: The result contains m ∆v, so the momentum equation is assumed to be one of the ingredients rather than the force equation.

mcqs.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 20 m/s is brought to rest in 0.10 s when it hits a wall. Using F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), which is given on the equation sheet, what is the average force on the car?

options.rationale: This is m ∆v, the change in momentum in kg m/s; the division by the time has been left out.
The mass has been divided by the time and the change in velocity omitted from the calculation.
A factor of one half has been introduced, as though the kinetic energy equation were involved.

mcqs.stem: In the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what does the quantity m ∆v represent?

options.text: the total momentum of the object
options.rationale: Drops the 'change in', so the object's whole momentum is used where only the change belongs.

options.text: the mass times the final velocity
options.rationale: ∆v is read as the final velocity rather than as the change in velocity.

options.text: the force acting on the object
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember 'force equals change of momentum' without the division by time.

options.text: the change in momentum of the object
options.rationale: The specification states that m ∆v = change in momentum, and its unit is kg m/s, not newtons.

mcqs.stem: The specification says that force equals the rate of change of momentum. What does 'rate of change of momentum' mean?

options.text: the change in momentum divided by the time taken
options.rationale: 'Rate of' means divided by time and 'change of momentum' means m ∆v, which together give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

options.text: the total momentum divided by the time taken
options.rationale: 'Rate of' is handled correctly but 'change of' is dropped, so the whole momentum is used.

options.text: the change in momentum multiplied by the time
options.rationale: Knows that time is involved but multiplies by it, which would make a longer collision a more forceful one.

options.text: the momentum an object has at a given moment
options.rationale: Reads 'rate' as 'at that instant', so no division is done at all and the answer is not a force.

mcqs.stem: A car is fitted with an air bag, which inflates in front of the driver during a crash. Why does the air bag reduce the force on the driver?

options.text: It makes the change in the driver's momentum much smaller.
options.rationale: The driver still goes from full speed to rest, so m ∆v is fixed; students attach the improvement to the wrong quantity.

options.text: It makes the driver's momentum change over a longer time.
options.rationale: The bag increases ∆t while m ∆v stays the same, so the rate of change of momentum, and therefore the force, is smaller.

options.text: It brings the driver to a stop far more quickly and safely.
options.rationale: Stopping quickly sounds like a safety benefit, but a shorter time gives a larger force.

options.text: It soaks up the force of the crash inside the bag of gas.
options.rationale: Treats force as a substance that can be stored, which is how padding is described in everyday language.

mcqs.stem: A gymnast lands on a thick crash mat rather than on the bare floor. Which explanation of the mat's effect is correct?

options.text: The mat reduces the gymnast's momentum on landing.
options.rationale: The gymnast arrives with the same mass and velocity either way, so the change in momentum is unchanged.

options.text: The mat stops the gymnast in a much shorter time.
options.rationale: 'Safe' is equated with 'stops you quickly', which is the reverse of how the mat works.

options.text: The mat increases the stopping time, so the force is less.
options.rationale: The mat squashes, so the same change in momentum happens over a longer ∆t and F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) is smaller.

options.text: The mat absorbs the force before it reaches the gymnast.
options.rationale: Force is imagined as something that flows and can be soaked up rather than as an interaction.

mcqs.stem: Two identical cars, each of mass 1200 kg, hit a wall at 20 m/s. Car A stops in 0.10 s. Car B has a crumple zone and stops in 0.50 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Car B's change in momentum is five times smaller than car A's.
options.rationale: Both cars go from 20 m/s to rest with the same mass, so m ∆v is 24 000 kg m/s for each; it is the time that differs.

options.text: The force on car B is the same, because the cars are identical.
options.rationale: Identical mass and speed fix the change in momentum, but the force also depends on the time, which is not the same.

options.text: The force on car B is five times greater than the force on car A.
options.rationale: The relationship is inverted: a longer stopping time is read as producing a bigger force.

options.text: The force on car B is one fifth of the force on car A.
options.rationale: The same 24 000 kg m/s spread over five times the time gives one fifth of the force: 48 000 N instead of 240 000 N.

mcqs.stem: A lorry of mass 12 000 kg is parked at the side of the road. What is its momentum?

options.text: zero, since its velocity is zero
options.rationale: p = m v, and any mass multiplied by a velocity of zero gives a momentum of zero.

options.text: 12 000 kg m/s, from its mass alone
options.rationale: The mass is quoted back as the momentum, treating momentum as something an object simply has.

options.text: very large, because its mass is large
options.rationale: Momentum is judged from mass alone, without the velocity being considered.

options.text: impossible to say without its weight
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the weight in newtons, not the mass, is what p = m v needs.
